title: A Giant Milky-Green Swirl Appeared in a Lake—From Space!
summary: Have you ever seen a giant green swirl from space? Astronauts did! In 2020, they looked down at Lake Skadar, which sits between Montenegro and Albania, and saw a huge milky-green spiral. It looks like a smoothie being stirred by a giant spoon. But it's not a monster or magic—it's sediment. That's tiny bits of rock, like limestone, that wash into the lake when snow melts in the mountains. The wind and water currents whip it into a vortex. Lake Skadar is the biggest lake in Southern Europe. It's about the size of 200,000 football fields! It's also a cryptodepression, which means most of the lake floor is below sea level. Millions of years ago, it was connected to the sea. Now, it's home to over 280 kinds of birds, including rare pelicans, and more kinds of freshwater snails than any other lake on Earth. There are even old shipwrecks and 600-year-old churches on its islands. Next time you see a swirl in your drink, think of Lake Skadar—nature's own giant mixing bowl!
why_it_matters: Next time you stir your drink, you're making a tiny vortex just like the giant one seen from space—nature's patterns are everywhere, even in your cup.

background_read: Lake Skadar sits between Montenegro and Albania, two countries in Europe near the coast. When snow melts in the mountains, it washes tiny rock pieces called sediment into the lake.
Over millions of years, parts of the lake that were once part of the sea are now home to many rare animals.
People from all over the world visit the lake to see its clear water, old churches on islands, and birds like pelicans.
Article_Structure: WHO: Astronauts looking from space and nature itself.
WHAT: A giant green swirl of sediment, like a stirred smoothie.
WHERE: Lake Skadar, a big lake between Montenegro and Albania.
WHY: Melting mountain snow washes limestone bits into the lake, and wind creates a vortex that makes the green pattern visible from space.

perspectives.description: They love studying the lake because it has more kinds of freshwater snails than anywhere else, and the cryptodepression makes it special.
They worry that too many visitors or pollution might harm the rare birds and the ancient shipwrecks.
They see the swirl from space as a reminder to visit the lake and see its clear water and old churches.
